why.From the col to the west, traversing the: When already high in the range on a multi-peak traverse, a party can reach the face from the west col across the icefield instead of walking in from the valley for this climb alone.

review.notes: Valley walk via Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek is the standard approach; the west-col line is traverse-party only, per stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side

why.Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge a: Parties who want reliable water and a more sheltered camp, or are tired or facing weather after the pass, stop at the lake instead of pushing on to the exposed ridge.

review.notes: Search confirmed the Downey/Bachelor approach only. The second entry is a camp choice, not a separate way in; reason is from stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it

problems: The non-primary 'way in' is a camp choice (lake vs ridge), not a distinct approach; consider whether it belongs in the picker.

why.Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes,: For a shorter walk to the pass, or to make a relaxed two-day trip with camping at Surprise Lake, accepting more climbing and a shadier, buggier trail.

review.notes: Tunnel Creek is the commonly described approach; Surprise Creek is the listed alternate, shorter, with camping at Surprise Lake.

why.North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49): Later in July and August when the river is low, or if the rough spur road to the Bedal trailhead is impassable or the climbers' path turn off the old trail worries the party.

review.notes: Reports favor Bedal Creek (no river crossings, though rough road and a missable junction); Cougar Creek is used after the river drops.

problems: Route prose calls Cougar Creek the standard approach while Bedal Creek is marked Most used; reports support Bedal as more popular, but some club trips use Cougar after mid-July.

why.Carrying through to the col camp above t: In settled weather with a sound glacier, a party carries overnight loads over the ice to camp at the col for a much shorter summit day, rather than stopping at the moraine.

review.notes: Moraine camp and col camp are both used, per park ranger notes and trip reports.

problems: The non-primary entry is a higher camp choice, not a separate way in.

why.Two camps: the lake meadows or the bench: When a shorter summit day matters more than shelter, a party goes on to the wind-exposed benches above the lake instead of camping at the meadows.

review.notes: Kindy Ridge approach confirmed, with lake basin camps; the bench camp reasoning is from stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them

problems: The non-primary entry is a camp choice, not a separate way in. A western approach (Slide Lake Trail off Illabot Creek Road) exists in reports but is not stored.

why.Early-season, snow in the basin: From the highway opening through June, when snow still buries the climbers' path in the basin and a party navigates by terrain, using firm morning snow to climb faster.

review.notes: Trip reports confirm early-season snow on the Blue Lake approach; same line, different conditions.

problems: The non-primary entry is the same line under snow, not a separate way in.

why.Early-season, snow in Spire Gully: From the highway opening through June, when Spire Gully still holds snow and the traverse is done on snow, with an axe and crampons for the extra firmness.

review.notes: Little web evidence specific to this route; written from stored notes.

problems: The non-primary entry is the same line under snow, not a separate way in.

why.Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loom: For the shortest walk and least total climbing, for parties who accept a drive about two hours longer and roughly 1,300 ft of uphill on the way out.
why.Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch Riv: When combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb, as a longer way round than the Andrews Creek trail.

review.notes: Andrews Creek, Chewuch River and Cathedral Driveway approaches confirmed; reasons from stored notes, with no web evidence for the Thirtymile use.
fromStoredNotes: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

why.Summer and autumn: the south side of the: Once the snow has gone, roughly June to October, when the gully can be scrambled dry from the Alpental road, a looser and lower-consequence outing than the winter climb.

review.notes: Winter approach from Summit West through Commonwealth Basin confirmed as the best and fastest; summer scramble described as a steep, loose outing.

problems: The two ways in are seasonal versions of one route rather than competing approaches; Most used reflects the winter climb.

why.The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass: To avoid the Chilliwack ford and the Imperfect Impasse, a party goes round via Whatcom Pass and crosses the river by cable car, accepting a longer walk and a brushy climbers' path.

review.notes: Reports confirm both the Easy Ridge to Perfect Pass line and the low orbit from Whatcom Pass.

problems: The non-primary way's notes repeat the Hannegan Pass trailhead walk and are muddled about how the low orbit connects; worth a tidy.

why.Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier: When the glacier is in good shape and the weather is settled, a party moves up to the saddle camp for a much shorter summit day instead of staying at the lake.

review.notes: Depot Creek approach confirmed from the Canadian side; reasons for the higher camp are from stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it

problems: The marked primary starts in Canada and crosses into the park at the boundary marker, not a port of entry; check lawfulness before it is shown as Most used.
The non-primary entry is a camp choice, not a separate way in.
Route id says SE rib but the route name is West Ridge (Beckey Route); the approach text may not match the name.
